B1:
Touched fires many times in one step, once for each body part (feet, legs and the HumanoidRootPart) and again as contacts repeat. Destroy doesn't stop handlers that are already queued for that frame, and with deferred events several Touched events are already in the queue before part:Destroy() takes effect. Each one adds 10 coins.
Fix: use a debounce flag that you set before granting, and disconnect.
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local part = script.Parent
local claimed = false
local conn
conn = part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if claimed then return end
    local char = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local plr = char and Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(char)
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not plr or not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    claimed = true
    conn:Disconnect()
    local ls = plr:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
    local coins = ls and ls:FindFirstChild("Coins")
    if coins then coins.Value += 10 end
    part:Destroy()
end)
```
Run this on the server. For many coins, use one tag-driven script with a per-coin claimed set.
B2:
With StreamingEnabled the client only has instances near the player. Far-away parts of Hotel, like the Door, haven't streamed in when the LocalScript runs, so indexing `.Door` errors. They can also stream out later and back in as a new instance, which breaks the connection.
Fix 1 (handle streaming): wait for the instance and react to stream-in and stream-out:
```lua
local hotel = workspace:WaitForChild("Map"):WaitForChild("Buildings"):WaitForChild("Hotel")
local door = hotel:WaitForChild("Door") -- may wait until in range (no timeout = may yield indefinitely)
```
Better, tag doors with CollectionService and use GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door") plus GetTagged. Connect when a door streams in and clean up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. That covers stream-in, stream-out and new doors.
Fix 2 (keep it loaded): make the door model always present on clients. Put it in a Model with ModelStreamingMode = Persistent (or Atomic for all-or-nothing loading), or call player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position) before using it.
Also consider moving Touched handling for doors to the server, which always has every part, and replicating the result.
B3:
Bugs:
1. It always returns PurchaseGranted, even when the pcall failed. The player is charged, the save failed and Roblox never retries, so they receive nothing.
2. There's no idempotency (no PurchaseId record). If the callback is retried (server shutdown, a timeout, an error after the save), coins are added twice.
3. Get then Set is not atomic. It races with other servers or saves and can overwrite or lose data. Use UpdateAsync.
4. `plr` can be nil if the player left, so `plr.UserId` errors. Use info.PlayerId and return NotProcessedYet if they aren't present.
5. It writes the DataStore directly while the session's player data, which is cached and saved later, may overwrite it. The coins should go through the player-data system.
6. The pcall result is ignored, and there's no check on info.ProductId.
Corrected behavior:
```lua
MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    if not plr then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        store:UpdateAsync(tostring(info.PlayerId), function(d)
            d = d or { Coins = 0, Receipts = {} }
            if d.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] then return d end -- already granted
            d.Coins += 100
            d.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] = true
            return d
        end)
    end)
    if not ok then warn(err) return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
Then update the live session or leaderstats.
B4:
1. Metatables don't replicate. Remote arguments are serialized and only the plain table data (Name, Ammo) is copied. The metatable and the functions are stripped, so the client gets an ordinary table with no Fire method, and `w:Fire()` calls nil. Functions themselves also can't be sent.
2. ServerStorage is never replicated to clients, so the client has no copy of Muzzle. Instance references that the receiver can't see arrive as nil.
Fix:
- Send plain data and rebuild the object on the client with a shared class module in ReplicatedStorage:
```lua
-- server
remote:FireClient(plr, { Name = "Rifle", Ammo = 30 }, muzzleClone)
-- client
local Weapon = require(ReplicatedStorage.Weapon)
remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(data, muzzle)
    local w = Weapon.new(data) -- setmetatable here
    w:Fire()
end)
```
- For the part, put it (or a clone) in ReplicatedStorage or Workspace before sending, so it exists on the client. Or just send an identifier and let the client find its own copy.
Also keep in mind that mixed or sparse tables and non-string keys can be altered by serialization.
B5:
workspace:Raycast's second argument is the direction and its length is the ray distance. `.Unit` makes it only 1 stud long, so the ray stops 1 stud from the origin and almost never hits anything. It can also hit your own character or gun first.
Fix: scale the direction to the range and exclude the shooter:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = { shooterCharacter }

local MAX = 300
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX   -- or (target - origin) for exact distance
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Also guard against target == origin, since the zero vector's .Unit is NaN.
B6:
When the last player leaves, or the server shuts down for an update or restart, the server closes. PlayerRemoving may fire, but the server doesn't wait for your yielding SetAsync to finish, so the process is killed mid-save. If the shutdown happens first, PlayerRemoving might not run at all for the remaining players.
Standard fix: use game:BindToClose, which gives you up to about 30 seconds before shutdown. In it, save every remaining player in parallel and wait until all saves finish. Have PlayerRemoving and BindToClose share one save function with a per-player "saving or saved" guard, so you don't double-save:
```lua
game:BindToClose(function()
    if RunService:IsStudio() then return end -- optional
    local pending = 0
    for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
        pending += 1
        task.spawn(function() savePlayer(p, true); pending -= 1 end)
    end
    while pending > 0 do task.wait() end
end)
```
Also:
- Use UpdateAsync with session locking, plus retries.
- Autosave every few minutes so a crash loses little.
- Check the request budget.
B7:
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UseAbility = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.UseAbility
local COOLDOWN = 2
local lastUse: {[Player]: number} = {}

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, abilityId)
    if typeof(abilityId) ~= "string" then return end
    local now = os.clock()
    local last = lastUse[player]
    if last and now - last < COOLDOWN then
        return -- spam/too early: silently ignore
    end
    lastUse[player] = now

    local char = player.Character
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    performAbility(player, abilityId) -- server-side effect/validation
end)

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    lastUse[player] = nil -- no leak
end)
```
The timestamp is set before the ability runs, so a yield inside the ability can't be raced. os.clock() is monotonic on the server. The client may show its own cooldown UI, but the server is authoritative.
B8:
```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData_v1")
local GEMS100 = 123456

local handlers = {
    [GEMS100] = function(data) data.Gems = (data.Gems or 0) + 100 end,
}

MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local handler = handlers[info.ProductId]
    if not handler then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end

    local player = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    if not player then
        return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet -- retried when they return
    end

    local granted = false
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        store:UpdateAsync("u_" .. info.PlayerId, function(data)
            data = data or { Gems = 0, Receipts = {} }
            data.Receipts = data.Receipts or {}
            if data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] then
                granted = true
                return nil            -- already processed: no write
            end
            handler(data)
            data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] = os.time()
            -- optionally trim old receipts to keep size bounded
            granted = true
            return data
        end)
    end)

    if not ok or not granted then
        warn("Receipt failed:", err)
        return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet
    end
    -- reflect in live session (if using cached profile, apply there instead)
    local ls = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
    if ls and ls:FindFirstChild("Gems") then ls.Gems.Value += 100 end
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local menu = script.Parent:WaitForChild("Menu")

local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
local SHOWN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)
local HIDDEN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 1.5, 0)
menu.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)

local current

local function open()
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    menu.Position = HIDDEN
    menu.Visible = true
    current = TweenService:Create(menu, info, { Position = SHOWN })
    current:Play()
end

local function close()
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    local t = TweenService:Create(menu, info, { Position = HIDDEN })
    current = t
    t.Completed:Connect(function(state)
        if state == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed and current == t then
            menu.Visible = false
        end
    end)
    t:Play()
end
```
The state check means that opening during a slide-out doesn't hide the menu afterwards. Optionally use In easing for the close.

B11:
```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local TAG = "KillBrick"
local connections: {[Instance]: RBXScriptConnection} = {}

local function onTouched(hit: BasePart)
    local model = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local hum = model and model:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if hum and hum.Health > 0 then
        hum.Health = 0
    end
end

local function setup(inst: Instance)
    if not inst:IsA("BasePart") or connections[inst] then return end
    connections[inst] = inst.Touched:Connect(onTouched)
end

local function cleanup(inst: Instance)
    local c = connections[inst]
    if c then
        c:Disconnect()
        connections[inst] = nil
    end
end

CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal(TAG):Connect(setup)
CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(cleanup)
for _, inst in CollectionService:GetTagged(TAG) do
    setup(inst)
end
```
The removed signal also fires when a tagged part is destroyed, so the table doesn't leak.

B13:
(a) Buying, client to server: use a RemoteEvent (BuyItem) or a RemoteFunction (client InvokeServer) if the UI needs an immediate success or fail result. The client sends only the intent (itemId). All validation (does the item exist, price from the server catalog, enough coins, rate limit, ownership) and the coin balance live on the server in its player-data object. The client never sends prices or balances.
(b) Updating the coin counter, server to client: either replicate the balance as state, for example a leaderstats IntValue, an attribute on the Player or a replicated Value that the UI listens to through GetPropertyChangedSignal/Changed, or send a RemoteEvent with FireClient(player, newBalance). The UI just displays what the server says.
Why not server-to-client InvokeClient: the server would yield waiting on the client. A malicious or laggy client can never return, which hangs the server thread forever. It can error, it errors if the player leaves, and it can return garbage. There's no reason to wait for a reply to a display update. One-way notifications should be RemoteEvents or replicated values. Only use RemoteFunctions client to server.
B14:
Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData, read with GetJoinData or GetLocalPlayerTeleportData) goes through the client. It is visible to the client and can be tampered with by exploiters (from a client-initiated teleport, or join data can be spoofed). It has a size limit and is lost if the teleport fails or the player rejoins directly. It's only suitable for non-authoritative hints: chosen map, party ID, UI state, or perhaps the chosen loadout as a preference that the destination validates against what the player owns.
DataStores are authoritative, persistent and secure on the server, but they are slower and have a write rate limit per key (about 6 seconds). A save then a load across a teleport needs session locking so the destination doesn't read stale data. MemoryStores (HashMap or SortedMap) are fast, cross-server and ephemeral with a TTL. They're good for a short-lived handoff like a match ticket or loadout keyed by userId, but they're not persistent and have quotas.
Choice: keep the coin balance only in DataStores. Save and release the session lock before teleporting, and have the destination load it (ProfileStore-style locking). Send the loadout as a validated reference: either in a MemoryStore HashMap entry keyed by userId or matchId with a short TTL, or in teleport data as a list of item IDs that the match server checks against the owned inventory from the DataStore. Never trust a coin amount from teleport data.
B15:
One Script per instance (610 copies) means 610 script instances, separate VMs, threads and memory, and slow replication of script copies. Changing door logic means editing or replacing every copy, which leads to drift and bugs. There's also no shared state (cooldowns, debouncing), and it gets harder to profile and secure. Copies also break when instances stream in and out.
Tag-driven: tag each instance (Door, Pickup, Turret) with CollectionService (set in Studio or with the Tag Editor). Then one module or system per tag:
- A server Script, or a ModuleScript loader in ServerScriptService, runs each system.
- Each system calls `setup(inst)` for CollectionService:GetTagged(tag), connects GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag) for new or cloned instances, and connects GetInstanceRemovedSignal(tag) for cleanup (disconnect connections, drop state from the table, use a Janitor/Trove per instance).
- Configuration goes in attributes on each instance (DoorSpeed, PickupValue, TurretRange), not in script copies.
- Turrets can share one Heartbeat loop that iterates over active turrets, instead of 60 loops. Throttle it, and possibly put it in Parallel Luau.
- Client-side visuals use the same pattern in a LocalScript. Under StreamingEnabled, the added signal fires when an instance streams in and the removed signal fires when it streams out, so the client automatically handles streamed instances. Tags replicate.
- Newly spawned instances (pickups respawning or a cloned turret) just need the tag. The system picks them up.
B16:
Give network ownership of the car to the driver. On the VehicleSeat's Occupant change on the server, call `chassisPart:SetNetworkOwner(player)` for the driver and SetNetworkOwner(nil) (the server) or auto when they exit. This gives responsive, lag-free driving, because the server simulating physics for a client-driven car would feel delayed. Unoccupied cars should be server-owned, so idle cars can't be pushed by a client.
Security risk: the owner's client simulates the car's physics and the server accepts its position and velocity. An exploiter can teleport the car, speed hack, fly, noclip through walls or checkpoints, or fling other players and cars, because physics from the owning client replicates.
What the server must still validate:
- Speed and acceleration caps, by comparing position deltas over time with the car's maximum speed.
- Position sanity: teleport detection, staying on or near the track, and no going through walls (raycast between samples).
- Checkpoint order and lap timing, done server-side with proper intervals and distances, so finishes aren't trusted from the client.
- Collisions or damage to others, applied on the server.
- Only the occupant gets ownership. Use SetNetworkOwnershipAuto off.
- Flag or reset violators by taking back ownership and moving the car back.
Keep remotes for boost or items server-validated with cooldowns.
B17:
Use UnreliableRemoteEvent for high-frequency, latest-value-wins data like aim direction and position. It doesn't resend or order packets, so a lost packet is simply replaced by the next one. That cuts queue pressure and head-of-line blocking.
Constraints:
- Delivery isn't guaranteed and ordering isn't guaranteed. Updates can be dropped or arrive out of order.
- The payload is small (about 900 bytes per call). Larger payloads are dropped.
- It's still rate-limited and exploitable like any remote.
How to handle them:
- Send absolute state (current aim and position), not deltas, so a drop doesn't matter.
- Include a sequence number or timestamp and ignore older packets on the receiver.
- Send compact data, for example a buffer or quantized values (aim as 2 int16 angles, position rounded), and send at a lower rate (10-20 Hz) or only when the value changed beyond a threshold.
- Interpolate on receivers.
- Keep critical events (fire, hit, reload, purchase) on a reliable RemoteEvent.
- The server validates every packet: types, NaN, plausible speed and position against the character, and a rate limit per player.
- Often the character's position is already replicated by physics ownership, so you only need to send aim.
B18:
Split the NPCs across Actors, for example 8-16 Actors each owning a batch of NPCs (not necessarily one per NPC). Put a Script under each Actor. Within each frame, do the expensive read-only work in parallel and apply results serially:
```lua
-- in a Script under an Actor
RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function(dt)
    -- parallel phase: raycasts, path scoring, target selection (reads only)
    local decisions = {}
    for _, npc in myNpcs do
        local r = workspace:Raycast(npc.origin, npc.dir * 50, params) -- allowed in parallel
        decisions[npc] = score(npc, r)
    end
    task.synchronize()
    -- serial phase: write to the DataModel
    for npc, d in decisions do npc.Humanoid:MoveTo(d.target) end
end)
```
Limitations to design around:
- In the parallel phase you can't modify most Instances or properties, fire most events or call many yielding APIs. Writes must happen after task.synchronize() (or in a separate serial step).
- Actors don't share Lua state. Each Actor has its own VM. Communicate with Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage or SharedTable, not shared module tables. Modules required in each Actor are separate copies.
- Each NPC's instances should be descendants of their Actor for correct ownership.
- The gain depends on the core count. There's overhead for sync and message passing, so batch instead of using thousands of tiny tasks.
- PathfindingService:ComputeAsync is yielding and not parallel-safe. Throttle it, or stagger path updates (for example, each NPC re-plans every 0.5-1 seconds, round-robin).
- Profile with the MicroProfiler. Often reducing per-frame work (frequency, distance-based LOD for far NPCs) gives as much benefit as parallelism.
B19:
Change in Workspace:
- StreamingEnabled = true.
- StreamingMinRadius around 64-128 (the content guaranteed around the player) and StreamingTargetRadius around 512-1024. The defaults (64 and 1024) are sensible starting points. Lower the target on dense maps.
- StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic, so memory is freed on low-memory devices. Default lets the engine decide.
- StreamingIntegrityMode = MinimumRadiusPause (or Default/PauseOutsideLoadedArea), so the player doesn't fall through unloaded terrain.
- Model-level ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must load all at once (buildings, vehicles), Persistent only for the few things scripts always need (sparingly, since they always use memory), and Default for the rest. Optionally Model.LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant imposters.
- Use player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(pos) before teleporting a player to a far location (on the server, or the client before a camera move).
Fixing scripts that assumed everything is loaded:
- Replace direct indexing with WaitForChild (with care) or FindFirstChild checks.
- Better, use CollectionService tags with GetInstanceAddedSignal/RemovedSignal so client logic attaches when instances stream in and cleans up when they stream out.
- Don't cache references to far parts forever. Handle nil.
- Server scripts are fine, since the server has everything.
- Test in Studio with streaming on and a low radius to find the breaks.
B20:
Cause: each SetAsync is a write request. With a 5-second autosave and 80 players that's about 960 writes per minute against a budget of about 60 + 80 x 10 = 860 per minute per server. On top of that, there's a per-key limit of about 1 write every 6 seconds. Writing the same key every 5 seconds exceeds it. Requests pile into the queue and the queue fills (error 302, "added to queue... queue full"), so writes, including leave saves, are dropped. SetAsync also blindly overwrites, which risks clobbering.
Better design:
- Cache data in memory per session. Mark it dirty when it changes.
- Autosave each player every 60-300 seconds, and only if dirty. Stagger the players, for example by spreading them over the interval (round-robin with an offset per player).
- Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (in parallel, waiting for completion).
- Use UpdateAsync with session locking and retries with exponential backoff, plus pcall.
- Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(Enum.DataStoreRequestType.SetIncrementAsync, or the Update type) before saving, and defer if it's low.
- Keep one key per player with all their data, not many keys.
- Use MemoryStore for data that needs fast cross-server updates, and OrderedDataStore updates less often.
- ProfileStore does all this for you.

B22:
The Input Action System (IAS) is a declarative, instance-based input system that replaces ContextActionService and raw UserInputService binding.
Three core instances:
- InputContext: a group of actions (a "mode", such as Gameplay, Menu or Vehicle). It has Enabled, Priority and Sink properties. It's placed somewhere the client sees it, for example under PlayerGui or in a LocalScript's tree.
- InputAction: one logical action (Jump, Sprint, Move). Its Type sets the value shape: Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, ViewportPosition and so on.
- InputBinding: maps a physical input to its parent action. It can be a KeyCode (keyboard, gamepad or mouse button), a UIButton (a GuiButton for touch), or composite directional keys (Up/Down/Left/Right) for 2D actions, with options such as Scale and PressedThreshold.
Signals: an InputAction fires Pressed and Released (for Bool actions) and StateChanged(newState) for any type. You can poll action:GetState(). You don't need to check device type, because every binding drives the same action.
Precedence: when the menu opens, enable a Menu InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player scripts' context and with Sink = true. Inputs bound in the Menu context are then consumed there and don't reach lower-priority contexts, like the default character controls that use IAS. You can also disable the gameplay context while the menu is open. Re-disable the menu context, or lower its priority, when it closes.
B23:
It's the UI Styling system (Style Editor), similar to CSS:
- StyleSheet: holds rules and tokens, usually in ReplicatedStorage (a design system).
- StyleRule: a child of a StyleSheet with a Selector string (CSS-like: class names like ".PrimaryButton", ClassName selectors like "TextButton", names with "#Name", descendant and child combinators like "Frame > TextLabel", and pseudo states like ":hover"/":pressed"). The properties it applies are set through StyleRule:SetProperty/SetProperties. Rules can nest, and Priority resolves conflicts.
- StyleLink: placed under a ScreenGui (or another UI root). Its StyleSheet property points to the sheet, and that is how styles reach the UI. Everything under that root gets the sheet's rules applied.
- StyleDerive: lets a sheet inherit or extend another sheet (themes such as light and dark).
- Classes: GuiObjects get class tags through their Tags (CollectionService tags with a "." in selectors).
Tokens: define them as attributes on the StyleSheet (for example `PrimaryColor = Color3`, `CornerRadius = UDim`) and reference them in rule properties as "$PrimaryColor". Change the attribute once and every rule that uses the token updates. A theme sheet can redefine the same tokens and be swapped through StyleDerive or StyleLink to restyle the whole UI.
Styles apply on top of default properties. A property set directly on an instance is overridden by rules depending on precedence, so leave styled properties at their defaults.
B24:
The check uses facial age estimation: a short selfie video in the Roblox app, processed by a third-party vendor (Persona), with the images deleted after processing. Users 13 and older can instead verify with a government ID. Without a check, chat features are off or restricted.
Age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+.
Restrictions: verified users can chat freely only with users in their own age group and the adjacent ones. For example, a 9-12 user can chat with under 9, 9-12 and 13-15, and a 16-17 user can chat with 13-15, 16-17 and 18-20. Larger gaps are blocked. Under-9s have chat off by default unless a parent enables it. Trusted Connections (verified 13+ users who know each other in real life, confirmed with a QR code or contact import) can chat across age groups. The rollout began in select countries in late 2025, and the age check became required for chat worldwide in early 2026. Experiences that use TextChatService get these rules automatically.
